evals.name: go-checkout-srp-and-security
evals.expected_output: Catches the client-controlled X-Admin header gating refunds (P1), PlaceOrder doing validation + pricing + persistence + notification, the volume-discount ladder re-implemented at two call sites when pricing.go already owns it (one collapsed finding), the unenforced Init-before-PlaceOrder coupling that silently zeroes tax, and OrderRepo.Query/Tx leaking the driver past the repository boundary — without claiming NewOrderRepo builds its own connection, without inflating the replaceable clock var to P1, and without inventing a finding against the clean pricing.go.
assertions: Flags RequireAdmin/RoleOf for deciding admin status from the caller-controlled X-Admin header, and rates it P1
Names the refund endpoint (or the privilege it grants) as what the forged header buys, rather than only observing that header-based auth is weak
Flags Service.PlaceOrder for combining validation, pricing, persistence and notification in a single function
Reports the duplicated volume-discount ladder — pricing.go's VolumeDiscountFraction re-implemented inline in PlaceOrder and again in Handler.quote — as ONE collapsed finding rather than one per site
Flags the Init-before-PlaceOrder temporal coupling, naming the consequence that a skipped Init leaves s.rates nil so tax is silently computed as zero
Flags OrderRepo.Query and/or Tx() for leaking the database driver past the repository boundary, naming handler.refund writing SQL in the HTTP layer as the misuse it enables
Flags the refund endpoint's non-idempotent UPDATE (no `refunded = false` guard, so a replay refunds twice) or its 200 {"refunded_cents": 0} response for an unknown id
Identifies processOrder or Tx() as a naming problem; if filed as a standalone finding it is rated P3
Does NOT claim NewOrderRepo opens or builds its own database connection — the *sql.DB is injected by the caller
Does NOT rate the package-level `clock = time.Now` var P1; it is an existing test seam and is at most P3
Does not fault pricing.go's own arithmetic or propose restructuring it — naming it as the canonical home the other two sites should call is correct
Reports at most one P1 finding; a report that assigns no P-levels at all does not satisfy this (having zero P1s with several P2s does)
Report follows REFERENCE.md: an 'N files reviewed, M issues found' header line and H3 findings tagged [P1]/[P2]/[P3] with a **Location:** line
Every finding carries a concrete 'done when' criterion verifiable by reading the diff
Total findings do not exceed 10

evals.name: ts-api-pattern-collapsing-and-api-shape
evals.expected_output: Flags the user endpoints returning the whole row including password_hash and reset_token (P1); collapses the three module-scope Pool constructions into one finding rather than three; flags the divergent shapes of getUser/getOrder/getSession and the raw snake_case row types leaking the schema; flags getSession's bare catch turning a database outage into a 401; leaves the pure money.ts alone.
assertions: Flags getUserHandler/updateUserHandler responding with the full UserRow including password_hash and reset_token, and rates it P1
Reports the module-scope `new Pool(...)` in users.ts, orders.ts and sessions.ts as ONE collapsed finding listing the affected files, not as a separate finding per file
Rates that module-scope Pool finding P2 or P3 — not P1, since vi.mock provides a seam in TypeScript
Does not claim the module-scope Pool makes the route modules untestable outright — acknowledges that module mocking provides a seam, even while faulting the design

Flags the divergent result shapes across sibling lookups (getUser returns null, getOrder throws NotFoundError, getSession returns {ok, data}), naming the cost to a consumer that wants to share code across them
Recommends the exported row interfaces stop being the response type across orders and sessions too, not only users.ts
Flags getSession's bare `catch { return { ok: false } }` for collapsing a database failure into 'no session', naming the consequence that an outage surfaces as 401 with nothing logged
Flags processOrder in orders.ts for a name that does not say it cancels an order
Raises no finding against money.ts, which is pure, total and single-purpose
Every P1 reported is a security finding; no more than two P1s in total

evals.name: py-clean-no-false-positives
evals.expected_output: Stays quiet. Dependencies are injected through a Protocol, functions hold one abstraction level, the error hierarchy carries actionable context, names say what they do. Correct output is zero findings, or at most one P3.
assertions: Reports zero findings, or at most one finding and that finding is P3
Claims no correctness, security or data-loss defect, under any severity vocabulary
Does NOT flag DEFAULT_RATES or MappingProxyType as shared mutable state — the view is read-only and TableRateSource copies it
Does NOT flag the RateSource Protocol as premature abstraction, nor ask for a second implementation to justify it
Does NOT flag pricing/__init__.py's re-exports as a module with unrelated exports
Does NOT ask for returned error values in place of the raised PricingError hierarchy — the idiom is applied consistently
States in words that the design is sound and names at least one thing carrying it — not merely a zero count
Does not pad the report with non-design housekeeping items such as __pycache__, .gitignore, or a missing lint/type-checker config filed as a finding

evals.name: py-worker-error-strategy-and-severity-floor
evals.expected_output: Separates real design defects (the import-time PaymentClient singleton reading os.environ, charge_customer collapsing declines and outages into None while retrying both, process_batch reading + validating + charging + reporting + emailing, PaymentClient.charge doubling as a refund call) from noise, keeps the singleton at P2 rather than P1, and does not file linter-owned findings about the length or nesting of process_batch.
assertions: Flags the module-scope `client = PaymentClient(api_key=os.environ[...])` for executing at import time, naming the consequence that importing the package fails without the env var and every consumer binds the same instance
Rates that singleton finding P2 or P3 — not P1, since monkeypatch.setattr provides a seam in Python
Flags charge_customer for catching bare Exception and returning None, naming the consequence that a card decline is retried like a network timeout and no caller can tell decline from outage from bug
Flags that charge_customer mints a fresh uuid4 idempotency key on every call, so re-running the nightly batch re-charges every customer
Flags process_batch for combining CSV reading, row validation, charging, report writing and emailing in one function
Flags PaymentClient.charge being reused for refunds by passing a charge_id where customer_id is expected and a negative amount
Flags report.handle_data for a name that does not say it totals charges per region, or for its `ValueError('bad input')` messages that name neither the row nor the field
Files no finding whose *claim* is that process_batch is too long or too deeply nested — naming its size while describing an SRP problem is fine, filing size itself as the defect is not
If the time.sleep backoff in charge_customer is raised at all, it is rated no higher than P3
Reports at most one P1 finding; a report that assigns no P-levels at all does not satisfy this (having zero P1s with several P2s does)

evals.name: py-store-upgrade-existing-state
evals.expected_output: Finds that migrations.run executes on every open with no version tracking, so an already-upgraded database crashes on its second start (duplicate column, then duplicate index); notices that the superseded customer index is still created by schema.init_db on every start and never dropped; leaves the IF NOT EXISTS schema and OrderRepo alone.
assertions: Flags migrations.run for running unconditionally on every open (app.open_database calls it each start) with nothing recording that it already ran, naming the consequence that the ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN raises a duplicate-column error on the second start so an already-upgraded database cannot restart
Identifies the same re-run hazard for the unguarded CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer_created (duplicate index error), either in the same finding or its own

Flags that the legacy idx_orders_customer is superseded by the composite index yet schema.init_db still creates it on every start and nothing drops it, so the table carries a redundant index that every write maintains
Frames the main finding as what happens to an existing database on upgrade or restart, not only as a missing migration framework in the abstract
Rates the restart-crash finding P1 or P2, not P3
Does not file a finding claiming schema.init_db's CREATE ... IF NOT EXISTS statements are unsafe to re-run, or flagging the audit_log table
Files no finding against OrderRepo's design (it is injected, parameterised and single-purpose)
Total findings do not exceed 10

evals.name: py-store-upgrade-diff-unchanged-migrations
evals.prompt: run `{FIXTURES}/py-store-upgrade-diff/setup.sh <empty-dir>`, cd into that directory, and review the code on the current branch (no path argument, so the review scopes to the branch's diff against main)
evals.expected_output: Reads past the two changed files to the unchanged migrations.py and app.py, and finds that the change redefines the orders table (total -> total_cents) and its index only in schema.init_db, which runs for new databases, while no migration was added and LATEST was not bumped, so an already-shipped database keeps the old shape and OrderRepo fails on it; leaves the fresh-database path alone.
assertions: Flags that the change alters the orders table (total -> total_cents) only in schema.init_db, which returns early for an existing database, so an already-shipped database never gets the total_cents column and the updated OrderRepo fails with no such column on it
Identifies that migrations.py, which is not part of the diff, is how existing databases are changed and that this change adds no migration entry and does not advance LATEST/user_version

Notes that fresh and upgraded databases end up with different schemas, including the index: new databases get idx_orders_customer_created while existing ones keep idx_orders_customer and nothing drops it
Names the failing sequence from an existing database's point of view (an instance created by the old release upgrades to this branch), not only the end state of the diff
Rates the missing-migration finding P1 or P2, not P3
Does not file a finding that creating a brand-new database is broken by this change
Total findings do not exceed 10
